Names cannot start with a number
Names are case-sensitive (Fish ≠ fish)
Avoid using R’s reserved words (like if, for, function)

title: 3. Understanding Data Frames in R
text:
What is a Data Frame? 📊
A data frame is a 2-dimensional table where: - Each column can hold different types of data (numbers, text, etc.) - All columns must have the same length - Each column has a name
Think of it like an Excel spreadsheet: - Rows are observations (e.g., individual fish) - Columns are variables (e.g., species, length, weight)

title: 1. Getting Started with R: Installation and First Steps
text:
Installing R and RStudio 💻

Step 1: Install R
First, you need to install R itself:

Go to CRAN (The Comprehensive R Archive Network)
Click on the link for your operating system:

Windows: “Download R for Windows” → “base” → Download the .exe file
Mac: “Download R for macOS” → Select the appropriate version
Linux: Choose your distribution and follow the instructions








Installation Tips




Windows users: Install R in the default directory (usually C:Files)
Mac users: You might need administrator privileges
Linux users: Consider using your package manager (apt, yum, etc.)





Step 2: Install RStudio
RStudio is an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) that makes working with R much easier:

Visit RStudio Downloads
Scroll down to “RStudio Desktop”
Download the free version for your operating system
Install following the default options







Important



Always install R first, then RStudio. RStudio needs R to work!

title: 1. Getting Started with R: Installation and First Steps
text:
Creating Your First R Project 📁
Projects help organize your work and make it portable. Here’s how to create one:

In RStudio, click File → New Project
Choose New Directory
Select New Project
Fill in:

Directory name (e.g., “my_fisheries_analysis”)
Where to create the project
Click “Create Project”



Understanding Project Structure
A well-organized project should have these folders:
my_fisheries_analysis/
├── data/          # Raw data files
│   ├── raw/      # Original, unchanged data
│   └── processed/ # Cleaned and processed data
├── R/            # R scripts
├── outputs/      # Results, figures, tables
│   ├── figures/  # Plots and visualizations
│   └── tables/   # Generated tables
└── docs/         # Documentation and reports






Best Practices for Project Organization




Keep raw data separate and unchanged
Use relative paths (project root as reference)
Name files and folders consistently
Include a README file explaining the project

title: 4. Base R vs Tidyverse: Why Packages Matter
section: Best Practices: When to Use Each Approach 📝
text:
Best Practices: When to Use Each Approach 📝

Use Base R When:

Working with very simple operations
Memory efficiency is crucial
Need maximum computational speed
Working with basic statistical functions
Teaching fundamental R concepts



Use Tidyverse When:

Working with data frames
Need readable and maintainable code
Performing data manipulation
Creating data pipelines
Working with dates and strings
Making plots with ggplot2







Pro Tip



You can mix base R and tidyverse approaches! Use what makes the most sense for each specific task.

title: 4. Base R vs Tidyverse: Why Packages Matter
text:
Key Takeaways 🎯

Readability: Tidyverse code is generally more readable and self-documenting
Consistency: Tidyverse functions work consistently together
Efficiency: Tidyverse often requires less code for complex operations
Learning Curve: Base R is simpler to start with but harder to master
Flexibility: Both approaches have their place in data analysis

title: 4. Base R vs Tidyverse: Why Packages Matter
text:
Next Steps 🚀

Practice converting your existing base R code to tidyverse
Learn more advanced tidyverse functions
Explore other tidyverse packages like purrr and tidyr
Develop your own style combining both approaches

Remember: The goal is not to completely replace base R, but to use the right tool for each job!
